title: Romani and Domari minority references

romania.method: Equal-size markers at representative interior points of census UATs with lmbRelRoma > 20. This is a visible selection, not a complete distribution or a majority-language fill. Percentages use known mother-tongue responses; ethnicity fields are not used. The lexical reference grast does not assert uniform dialect usage at every point.
romania.sourceTerms: INS RPL 2021 data mapped by ISPMN; no blanket Glottography CC BY license is asserted for this supplement.

westernRomani.evidence: Nominative Sinti graj plus Hameln accusative grajes; a documented reference community, not a population maximum.

linguisticDistinction: Romani varieties share the Armenian grast loan set. Domari is a distinct Indo-Aryan language; its documented horse word is researched separately.

syrianDomari.alternateTranscription: agorà (Matras and Kelzi 2024); à represents vowel quality

syrianDomari.displayNote: The Damascus reference repeats Aleppo agōra with the same unboxed Domari caption and word style. This is an explicitly shared lexical reference, not new Damascus lexical evidence.

iraqiKawliya.status: Modern community-specific horse lexeme not verified; no word or language boundary has been invented.
iraqiKawliya.communityPresence: Al-Qadissiya and around Baghdad, Basra and Mosul are documented in the 2017 community report, with heterogeneous identities discussed in later fieldwork.

historicalComparison.informantOrigin: Altun Kupri, described as in the Baghdad pashalik; not Baghdad city
historicalComparison.caveat: This historical record cannot establish present-day Kawliya vocabulary, language identity or a universal shift to Arabic.

mapRepresentation.name: Kawliya (Iraq)
mapRepresentation.notes: No modern Iraqi Kawliya-specific word for horse has been verified. The open marker records documented community presence only and is not assigned a horse-word origin colour. Newbold (1856) recorded asp from a Duman informant from Altun Kupri; that historical northern Iraqi record is not substituted for present-day Kawliya speech in southern Iraq. Iraqi communities have varied language practices and identities.
mapRepresentation.locationNote: Approximate Diwaniyah regional reference, not an exact village coordinate, boundary or current population estimate. Reuters reported from Al-Zuhoor village, Diwaniya, in 2018; Minority Rights Group documents communities in Al-Qadissiya.

balkanAndEasternReferences.method: Twelve equal-size approximate town locators from the primary RMS inventory. They document language-reference communities, not current population counts, density or complete distribution. Romanian census selection and linguistic sample selection are explicitly different. Displayed grast is a reference form; individual word-evidence qualifications are retained below.

markerPresentation: Romani, Sinti Romani and both Domari word references use the same unboxed caption and word style. Damascus repeats the Aleppo lexical reference with a leader to its community marker; it has no place-name caption or background box. A neutral open Kawliya marker near Diwaniyah documents community presence without assigning an unverified horse word or origin colour.
